newsitem.title: USA: INSTANT VIEW - U.S. Sept retail sales up 0.7 pct.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW - U.S. Sept retail sales up 0.7 pct.

text.p: Following are comments from U.S. economists after the Commerce Department said September retail sales rose 0.7 percent, following a revised 0.2-percent decrease in August.
Excluding autos, sales were up 0.4 percent.
U.S. economists in a Reuters survey had expected a 0.2-percent rise in overall sales and a 0.3-percent increase minus cars.
CHRISTOPHER LOW, SENIOR ECONOMIST, HSBC MARKETS INC: "I think (the reports) are quite bullish, especially retail sales."

"When you do an analysis of retail sales for GDP you have to look at the ex-auto figures. We had a big downward revision in August and I think it will leave most analysts thinking perhaps consumption is a bit weaker than they thought in the (third) quarter in terms of GDP," Low concluded.

CHERYL KATZ, SENIOR ECONOMIST, MERRILL LYNCH: "All-in-all, its still obvious that consumer spending has slowed considerably from the first half of 1996 and will probably come in near one percent in the second half.
"Thsi information suggests that the momentum has slowed. We're probably talking about slightly under two percent (GDP) growth in the third quarter."
WALDO BEST, SENIOR ECONOMIST, BZW GOVERNMENT SECURITIES:
"When you factor in those large downward revisions to last month's retail sales it's pretty much on top of expectations.

"The headline number looks really strong at up 0.7 percent but when you take into account that they really gutted last month's number the real story is the revision to last month's figure rather than any real strength in September," Best said.
ROBERT BRUSCA, CHIEF ECONOMIST AT NIKKO SECURITIES CO:
"Retail sales were strong in September, but, if you take into account the downward revision from the prior month, that takes away a lot from this increase," Brusca said.
"This report shows there is more life, but nothing very special."
Brusca also commented the market is waiting for the September Consumer Price Index, due out on Tuesday, to get a better sense of the underlying inflation pressure.
